questiontext.text: Radar shows a developing line of thunderstorm cells over the northern sub-area of the FIR. Visual inspection and reflectivity coverage suggest the cells occupy roughly 60% of the sub-area, with discernible gaps between adjacent cells. Intensity is moderate. What message should the MWO issue?

generalfeedback.text: Rationale: Coverage between 50% and 75% with discernible separation between cells is OCNL TS — an AIRMET phenomenon. FRQ requires coverage greater than 75% with little or no separation. The cells do not need to be embedded, obscured, or in a squall line to fall under AIRMET, so a SIGMET is not warranted. "No message" misses the operational hazard to low-level traffic crossing the area.

answer.text: An AIRMET for OCNL TS over the affected sub-area.
A SIGMET for FRQ TS — once coverage exceeds 50%, FRQ applies.
A SIGMET for EMBD TS, on the basis of the line structure.
No message — moderate-intensity cells with gaps do not trigger any product.

questiontext.text: Which of the following phenomena triggers an AIRMET but has no SIGMET equivalent at any intensity?

generalfeedback.text: Rationale: Cloud ceilings below 1000 ft, sustained surface winds ≥ 30 kt, visibility below 5 km, and extensive mountain obscuration are AIRMET-only phenomena — they describe the low-level environment and have no SIGMET counterpart. Severe icing and embedded thunderstorms are SIGMET phenomena (with AIRMET counterparts at lower intensity, MOD ICE and ISOL/OCNL TS). Volcanic ash is exclusively a SIGMET (WV) phenomenon.

answer.text: Cloud ceilings below 1000 ft over an extensive area.
Severe icing with freezing rain.
Embedded thunderstorms over the FIR.
Volcanic ash drifting through the FIR.

questiontext.text: The model's icing-potential field is moderate-to-strong over a stratus layer between 5,000 and 8,500 ft. A pilot report at 7,000 ft describes the icing as "moderate" with no reference to freezing rain. The synoptic situation supports persistent moderate icing for the next three hours. Which message should the MWO issue?

generalfeedback.text: Rationale: Both model output and the PIREP describe the icing as moderate, and the cloud is stratiform (not convective), so MOD ICE is the correct AIRMET phenomenon. SEV ICE would require a severe PIREP or unambiguous model indication of severe icing — not present here. The presence or absence of FZRA is a qualifier on a severe case, not a standalone trigger. Doing nothing leaves a known low-level hazard un-warned.

answer.text: An AIRMET for MOD ICE.
A SIGMET for SEV ICE, because stratus icing should always be promoted to severe in winter.
A SIGMET for SEV ICE FZRA, because freezing rain is a winter default assumption.
No message — pilot reports of moderate icing are not actionable on their own.

questiontext.text: A strong synoptic pressure gradient is forecast to drive sustained 10-minute mean surface winds of 32 kt across a broad sub-area of the FIR for the next 4 hours. Gusts will be higher. Which product covers the en-route hazard to general aviation across the affected area?

generalfeedback.text: Rationale: Sustained surface winds ≥ 30 kt over an extensive area is an AIRMET phenomenon (SFC WSPD ≥30KT) and has no SIGMET equivalent. The aerodrome warning is a separate product, scoped to the airport itself, and is covered in Lesson 4 — an AD WRNG does not warn the en-route GA pilot crossing the FIR. A WS WRNG addresses runway-specific wind shear, not large-scale surface winds.

answer.text: An AIRMET for SFC WSPD ≥30KT over the affected sub-area.
A SIGMET for severe surface winds, since 32 kt is well above 30 kt.
An AD WRNG, because surface winds primarily affect aerodromes.
A WS WRNG, because the winds are likely to cause runway-shear conditions.

name.text: L3-Q05 — AIRMET vs SIGMET in a borderline case

questiontext.text: A mountain-wave forecast shows downdrafts peaking at exactly 3.0 m/s along the lee slopes, with accompanying severe turbulence forecast in patches. Which warning is appropriate?

generalfeedback.text: Rationale: The SEV MTW threshold is downdraft ≥ 3.0 m/s or accompanying severe turbulence. Both conditions are present here, so SIGMET is the correct call — the boundary is inclusive, not exclusive. Issuing an AIRMET for MOD MTW would under-warn the hazard. Issuing both an AIRMET and a SIGMET for the same phenomenon over the same area violates the one-phenomenon-one-message principle.

answer.text: A SIGMET for SEV MTW — the 3.0 m/s threshold is inclusive and the accompanying SEV turbulence also qualifies on its own.
An AIRMET for MOD MTW — 3.0 m/s is the upper bound of the MOD band.
Both an AIRMET (for the wave) and a SIGMET (for the turbulence) over the same area.
No warning — the model is at the boundary, so the case should be left to the routine SIGWX chart.

questiontext.text: An MWO trainee asks why the IMS issues an AIRMET for visibility <5 km in haze even though the TAFs for the affected aerodromes already mention reduced visibility. What is the correct explanation?

generalfeedback.text: Rationale: The "not already in the forecast" exemption refers specifically to a low-level area forecast covering the same FIR or sub-area at AIRMET intensity — typically a GAMET. TAFs are aerodrome forecasts, not low-level area forecasts; they do not exempt the MWO from issuing an AIRMET for an en-route visibility hazard. Israel does not produce a GAMET, so the exemption almost never applies and the AIRMET is issued whenever the phenomenon and intensity criteria are met. The exemption is not a "discretionary" or "tradition" clause — it is a specific carve-out tied to the existence of a covering area forecast.

answer.text: The exemption applies only when a low-level area forecast (e.g., GAMET) covers the FIR at AIRMET intensity; TAFs are aerodrome forecasts and do not satisfy the exemption.
The exemption is purely discretionary — the MWO can choose to issue the AIRMET or rely on the TAFs.
The exemption never applies to visibility, only to ceiling and surface wind AIRMETs.
The exemption is an IMS-only tradition; in other countries the TAFs would be sufficient.

name.text: L3-Q07 — AIRMET vs SIGMET by coverage

questiontext.text: Thunderstorms are forecast over about 60% of a FIR sub-area with gaps between cells. Which product and qualifier apply?

generalfeedback.text: Rationale: 60% coverage with gaps is OCNL (50–75%), an AIRMET qualifier. FRQ (>75%, little or no separation) is what would promote it to a SIGMET. The choice is driven by coverage fraction, not by cell intensity or reflectivity.

answer.text: AIRMET, OCNL TS — 50–75% coverage with gaps.
SIGMET, FRQ TS — any thunderstorm coverage is a SIGMET.
AIRMET, ISOL TS — coverage below 50%.
No message — thunderstorms are only ever in the TAF.

questiontext.text: Widespread visibility below 5 km in haze is forecast across a low-level FIR sub-area. Why is this an AIRMET phenomenon with no SIGMET equivalent?

generalfeedback.text: Rationale: Visibility below 5 km (like ceiling below 1000 ft, surface wind ≥30 kt, and extensive mountain obscuration) is inherently a low-level, general-aviation/rotorcraft hazard, so it appears only on the AIRMET list. SIGMET phenomena are the higher-intensity en-route hazards to all aircraft. Cause (haze, fog, dust, precip) does not matter — the effect on visibility does.

answer.text: Low-level visibility is an AIRMET-only phenomenon affecting GA/rotorcraft; SIGMET has no equivalent.
It should be a WS SIGMET because all visibility hazards are SIGMETs.
It is only ever an aerodrome warning, never an AIRMET.
Haze is not a recognised obscuration, so no message is issued.
